text:
Take \(c=1\) and \(m_\nu \approx 0\). Since the pion is initially at rest, the \(\mu^+\) and \(\nu\) have equal and opposite momenta.

For a two-body decay \(M \to m + 0\):

\[
E_\nu=\frac{M^2-m^2}{2M},\qquad 
K_\mu=E_\mu-m=\frac{(M-m)^2}{2M}
\]

With \(M=139.6\ \text{MeV}\), \(m=105.7\ \text{MeV}\):

\[
E_\nu=\frac{139.6^2-105.7^2}{2(139.6)}=29.8\ \text{MeV}
\]

\[
K_\mu=\frac{(139.6-105.7)^2}{2(139.6)}
=\frac{33.9^2}{279.2}=4.12\ \text{MeV}
\]

Check: \(4.12+29.8 \approx 33.9\ \text{MeV}=M-m\).

So \(K(\mu^+)\approx 4.12\ \text{MeV}\), \(K(\nu)\approx 29.8\ \text{MeV}\).

Answer: A
